summary:
Mars Base Alpha is a Mars base management game that kids aged 7–12 can play in their browser. The player becomes the base commander for 14 sols (Martian
  days) and has to balance power, oxygen, water, food, the radiation shield and crew morale. Every choice has a gain and a cost; no choice is free. If any
  gauge drops to zero, the mission ends. Each of the 14 sols is tied to a real space weather day from 3–16 May 2024, taken from NASA DONKI. Kids learn
  firsthand how a solar flare affects their shield and oxygen decisions. After every choice, an info card shows its source. The game is available in Turkish
  and English and needs no installation or account.
details:
What it does

Mars Base Alpha is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. The player becomes the commander of a small Mars base for 14 sols (Martian days). First they choose one of three real landing sites: Elysium Planitia, Jezero Crater or Arsia Mons. Each site changes the starting conditions. Then every sol brings a decision card with two options. Before clicking, each option shows which of the six systems (power, oxygen, water, food, radiation shield, crew morale) it will raise and which it will lower. No choice is free. If any system reaches zero, the mission fails. After each decision, an Info Corner card explains the real NASA technology behind it, such as MOXIE on Perseverance, the ISS Water Recovery System or Curiosity's RAD, and shows its source. At the end, a mission report shows the result and, if the mission failed, which system ran out.

How it works and how it uses NASA data

Each of the 14 sols is tied to a real space weather day from 3–16 May 2024, taken from NASA DONKI. On sol 4 the player meets a real X4.5 solar flare. On sol 8 they meet the real Kp 9 geomagnetic storm of 10 May 2024, the strongest in about 20 years. A panel in the corner shows the real date and source. The landing-site maps come from NASA Mars Trek (Viking MDIM2.1 mosaic) and the backgrounds are NASA photos. The Info Corner facts are based on NASA OSDR studies (OSD-895, OSD-984, OSD-1018), RadLab radiation data and NASA mission information. These are archived records built into the game, not live data, so the game works offline. All raw NASA downloads are kept in the /data folder of our repository so anyone can check them.

How we built it, step by step

1. We chose the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge and studied what it asks for: real trade-offs, real NASA data and sources shown inside the tool.

2. Our team wrote the game design: a Mars setting, 14 sols, six resources and their real NASA counterparts, a landing-site choice, decision cards and an Info Corner after each choice.

3. We collected NASA resources. Our team got a NASA API key and downloaded the OSDR studies. We pulled space weather events from DONKI, maps from Mars Trek, radiation data from RadLab and photos from the NASA Image and Video Library.

4. We built the game as a single web page, following our design and our interface mockups, in Turkish and English.

5. We tested the balance. Our first version was unfair: 94% of games were lost to power alone, so the game was not teaching trade-offs. We simulated all 524,288 possible playthroughs (19 decisions × 2 options) and rebalanced until each of the six systems can end the mission. Random play now wins about 44% of the time; careful play wins.

6. We checked every fact. All 19 Info Corner cards were compared with NASA sources, and 13 of them were corrected.

Benefits for kids

- Systems thinking: kids see that changing one system affects the others. More oxygen means less power.

- Learning by doing: instead of memorizing facts, they make their own decisions and live the results.

- Decision-making: they notice that every choice has a cost and that good decisions take thought.

- Learning from failure: if the mission fails, the report shows which system ran out, so they try again with a new strategy.

- Curiosity for real science: after every decision they learn about a real NASA technology, which links play to real science.

- For every age: it is designed for ages 7–12, but because it is a game, parents, teachers and older players can enjoy it and learn from it too. It also works as a group activity in class.

Intended impact

Space content for kids often stays at the level of posters and facts. We want every child who plays to understand that a space base is an engineering system where every gain has a cost, the same kind of decisions NASA mission planners make. Because the game needs no installation, account or internet connection and is free and open source in two languages, any school or family with a browser can use it.

Creativity

The game does not use invented events. It replays a real historic solar storm on a Martian base, so a child connects a real day on the Sun with a decision they make themselves.

Tools, languages and software

HTML5, CSS and plain JavaScript (no frameworks, no build step); Google Fonts (Saira); NASA public APIs and Mars Trek map tiles for data collection; GitHub for hosting the code. We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant; its use is described in the Use of SI section and in our README. The code is open source under the MIT License.

What our team considered

- Age: short sentences, large buttons and only two options per decision, with icons that show the effects before the player clicks.

- Accuracy: only real NASA data and checked facts, with sources shown inside the game.

- Fairness: every system matters, which we measured instead of guessing.

- Access: free, offline, bilingual and playable in any browser.

- Honesty: archived data is not shown as live data, and SI use is stated openly.

Next steps

Playtests in classrooms, a Moon outpost mode and live DONKI space weather alerts.

NASA OSDR - OSD-895 (EDEN ISS greenhouse biomass)
NASA OSDR - OSD-984 (muscle and cosmic radiation)
NASA OSDR RadLab - ISS radiation dose data (DosTel)
NASA Image PIA26680 - Curiosity postcard from Mount Sharp (game background)
NASA Image PIA24264 - Mastcam-Z first 360-degree panorama (game background)
NASA Image PIA24937 - Curiosity Navcam postcard (game background)
NASA Curiosity rover (RAD radiation, REMS weather)
NASA Perseverance rover (MOXIE oxygen, MEDA weather)
NASA ECLSS - Environmental Control and Life Support Systems
NASA International Space Station (Veggie, ARED exercise, Zvezda leak)
NASA HERA - Human Exploration Research Analog
